title: Your Frozen Paratha May Be Wrecking Your Gut. A 124,000-Person Study Just Singled Out Ultraprocessed Grains.
excerpt: The largest global study of its kind found that ultraprocessed grain intake nearly doubled the risk of inflammatory bowel disease. Fresh bread and rice were protective. The implications for diaspora kitchens are enormous.
body:
The largest global analysis of its kind has drawn a straight line between ultraprocessed grain consumption and inflammatory bowel disease — and the findings carry a pointed warning for every diaspora kitchen that has swapped fresh chapati for a freezer full of ready-made parathas.

Published in the June issue of the American Journal of Gastroenterology, the study drew on data from 124,590 participants across 21 countries enrolled in the Prospective Urban Rural Epidemiology (PURE) study. Led by Dr. Neeraj Narula, a gastroenterologist and associate professor of medicine at McMaster University in Hamilton, Ontario, the research tracked dietary patterns and disease outcomes over nearly a decade.

## The Numbers

The headline finding is stark. After adjusting for age, sex, smoking, eating habits, and physical activity, participants consuming 19 grams or more of ultraprocessed grains per day had an 86 per cent higher risk of developing IBD compared with those eating less than 9 grams daily (hazard ratio 1.86). The association held for both Crohn’s disease and ulcerative colitis.

At higher consumption levels, the numbers became alarming. Participants eating five or more servings of ultraprocessed food per day had nearly four times the risk of developing IBD compared with those eating less than one serving (hazard ratio 3.95).

But the study also offered a counterpoint that matters enormously. Fresh bread and rice consumption were associated with lower IBD risk. “Not all grains carry risk,” Dr. Narula told Medscape Medical News. “Minimally processed grains like fresh bread and rice were associated with lower risk even.”

## What Counts as Ultraprocessed Grain

The distinction matters because it separates the grain itself from what industrial processing does to it. Ultraprocessed grain products include packaged sliced bread loaded with emulsifiers and preservatives, instant noodles, breakfast cereals with added flavourings and colours, biscuits, cookies, and frozen dough products.

A fresh chapati made from stone-ground wheat flour, water, and a pinch of salt is a minimally processed grain product. A frozen paratha from a supermarket shelf, with its hydrogenated vegetable oil, stabilisers, flavour enhancers, and preservative system, is an ultraprocessed one. The grain is the same. The processing is not.

The mechanisms are still being studied, but the PURE researchers point to several pathways. Additives used in ultraprocessed grains — emulsifiers, artificial sweeteners, and certain preservatives — have been shown in laboratory studies to disrupt the gut microbiome and damage the intestinal barrier. The refining process itself strips fibre and nutrients that feed beneficial gut bacteria. And the high glycaemic load of many ultraprocessed grain products can trigger inflammatory cascades.

## The Diaspora Kitchen Problem

The finding lands with particular force in NRI households across North America, the UK, and the Gulf. The traditional Indian kitchen is built on grains: roti from freshly kneaded atta, rice cooked from raw grain, fermented dosa and idli batter prepared overnight, handmade puris for special occasions.

But the convenience economy has reshaped diaspora eating habits. The frozen food aisle in any Indian grocery store in Edison, Artesia, or Brampton tells the story: stacks of frozen parathas, ready-to-heat naan, instant dosa mixes, and microwave-ready rice packets. For dual-income families working long hours, these products have become weeknight staples.

The PURE data suggests this convenience may come at a measurable cost. India itself has seen a dramatic rise in IBD incidence over the past two decades, a trajectory that correlates closely with the penetration of packaged and ultraprocessed foods into the Indian diet.

## What Practical Steps Look Like

The study does not call for eliminating all processed grains. It draws a clear line between minimally processed and ultraprocessed, and the practical implications are straightforward.

Fresh roti made from whole wheat flour at home is protective. The same roti from a frozen packet with a 12-month shelf life is not. Rice cooked from raw grain is protective. Instant rice and flavoured rice packets are in a different category. Idli batter fermented overnight from soaked urad dal and rice carries the probiotic benefits of natural fermentation. An instant idli mix reconstituted with water does not.

For NRI families navigating busy schedules, the middle ground may be weekend batch-cooking — making and freezing fresh rotis, preparing dosa batter in larger quantities, cooking rice in bulk. The grain stays the same. What changes is who controls the processing.

“By identifying specific dietary factors such as ultraprocessed grains that contribute to disease development, this study provides a foundation for targeted dietary recommendations and public health initiatives aimed at reducing the burden of IBD worldwide,” the PURE team concluded. For the diaspora, the targeted recommendation is simple: cook your grains the way your grandmother did.
